content_units: Heating Fault Snapshot for Your Dublin Townhouse

A boiler that   loses pressure every 10–14 days   plus   one radiator cold at the top   most often points to a   small sealed-system issue   rather than a major emergency. The least disruptive first step is usually   one visit from an RGII-registered heating engineer who also handles hydronic heating diagnostics  ; that covers the boiler side and most radiator/pressure faults in one appointment.
Working context
- 120 m² townhouse, Dublin, sealed wet heating system assumed.
- Budget target for first diagnostic visit:   up to €180  .
- Priority:   minimum disruption   with a baby at home.
Likely Faults and First-Visit Priority
Likely cause   Why it fits your symptoms   Disruption   Typical first fix   Best first trade
Air trapped in upstairs radiator   Cold at the top is a classic sign; upstairs rads collect air first   Low   Bleed radiator and re-pressurise system   Heating engineer

Small leak on heating circuit   Pressure dropping every 10–14 days strongly suggests slow water loss at valve, joint, rad, or pipework   Low to Medium   Visual leak check; tighten/replace valve part; pressure test   Heating engineer
Expansion vessel losing charge   Can cause repeated pressure swings and top-ups, especially after heating cycles   Medium   Check vessel charge; recharge or replace vessel   Heating engineer
Pressure relief valve passing water   If discharge pipe outside is dripping, boiler may be shedding pressure   Low   Check PRV outlet; replace faulty PRV if needed   Heating engineer
Radiator balancing / weak circulation   One upstairs radiator may stay partly cold if system is unbalanced or lockshield/TRV issue   Low   Free TRV pin; rebalance system   Heating engineer

Hidden pipe leak under floors/walls   Less likely if loss is slow and no staining, but possible if all visible parts look dry   Medium to High   Pressure test, isolate zones, leak tracing   Heating engineer first, plumber if pipe repair needed
Best route for your situation
Book a heating engineer first  , not a general plumber, if you can find one who explicitly covers:
- boiler diagnostics
- sealed heating system pressure loss
- radiator/TRV balancing and bleeding
- expansion vessel / PRV checks
Why:
- One person can usually check   boiler, vessel, PRV, pressure gauge behavior, radiator air, TRVs, and balancing   in a single visit.
- A plumber is more useful   only if the engineer identifies a pipework leak or valve/body replacement outside the boiler  .
Low-Disruption Checks to Do Before Booking
Do these in order, ideally with the heating off and the system cooled for at least 30–60 minutes.
Step   Action   What to check   Expected result
1   Note current boiler pressure   Cold system pressure is often around   1.0–1.5 bar   on many homes   Stable reading to compare later

2   Check for obvious leaks   Look under boiler, around radiator valves, towel rails, ceilings below upstairs rad, and near hot press/cylinder area if present   No dampness, staining, or green/white crust
3   Look at external discharge pipe   Outside wall near boiler: any regular dripping can indicate PRV passing water   Should be dry when system idle
4   Check the cold-top radiator valve heads   Ensure TRV is open; if possible gently confirm pin is not stuck   Radiator should begin heating more evenly
5   Bleed only the cold-top radiator   If air comes out first, that supports trapped air   Heat should improve after bleeding
6   Recheck boiler pressure after bleeding   Bleeding reduces system pressure slightly   Top up only to normal cold pressure if needed
7   Monitor for 3–7 days   Photograph gauge morning/evening and after heating cycles   Helps engineer diagnose vessel vs leak
8   Stop repeated top-ups if pressure keeps falling fast   Frequent fresh water adds oxygen and can worsen corrosion   Book service promptly
Simple interpretation
-   Cold at top, warm at bottom  : usually   air  .
-   Cold at bottom, warm at top  : more often sludge/balancing.
-   Pressure falls only after heating then cool-down  : often   expansion vessel / PRV  .
-   Pressure falls steadily even when boiler stays off  : more suggestive of a   leak  .
Least-Disruptive Troubleshooting Sequence
1) Try one controlled radiator bleed
- Turn heating off and let system cool.
- Put a cloth/container under the upstairs radiator bleed point.
- Open the bleed screw slowly.
- If you hear   air hiss  , let it vent until water runs steadily, then close.
- Check boiler pressure afterward; if low, top up only to the normal cold setting shown in your boiler manual or pressure label.
2) Do a quiet visual leak walk-through
- Check radiator valve nuts and tails for tiny beads of water.
- Run dry tissue around suspect joints.
- Look for pinhole clues: rust marks, skirting swelling, faint staining, musty smell.
3) Check whether the issue is radiator-specific
- Make sure the TRV is fully open.
- If the radiator still stays cold at the top after bleeding, the valve, balancing, or circulation may need adjustment.
4) If pressure continues to drop, book a heating engineer
- Ask for a   diagnostic-only first visit   within your €180 cap.
- Request   no invasive work without approval  .
- Ask them to bring kit for   expansion vessel recharge, PRV assessment, radiator balancing, and leak isolation tests  .
What to Ask When Booking the Service
Use wording like this:
- “We have a sealed heating system in a townhouse in Dublin. The   boiler loses pressure every 10 to 14 days   and   one upstairs radiator stays cold at the top  .”
- “We want the   least disruptive first diagnostic visit  , as we have a baby at home.”
- “Can you diagnose   pressure loss, expansion vessel, PRV, radiator air/TRV, and balancing   in one callout?”
- “Are you   RGII registered   if the boiler case needs to be opened or gas-side checks are needed?”
- “Can you keep the   initial diagnostic visit within €180   unless you get approval first?”
- “Do you charge separately for   parts, repressurising, vessel recharge, PRV replacement, or radiator valve work  ?”
- “If it turns out to be a hidden pipe leak, do you handle leak tracing/repair or would that need a plumber?”
- “Can you give a   2-hour arrival window   and a likely visit length?”
- “Can you work with   minimal system downtime   on the day?”
Good booking outcome
Choose the provider who answers   yes   to most of these:
- Can diagnose both   boiler pressure loss   and   radiator heating fault
- Comfortable with   sealed-system components
- Will do   diagnostics first
- Will respect a   spend cap
- Can explain whether a second trade is actually needed
Practical Recommendation for Your Home
Most likely least-disruptive path:
1. Bleed the upstairs radiator once.
2. Check pressure and visible leaks.
3. If pressure still drops, book   one heating engineer first  .
4. Call a plumber only if they confirm a   pipework/valve leak repair   outside normal heating-engineer scope.
When to skip DIY and book immediately
- Pressure drops from normal to very low in   1–3 days
- Boiler locks out repeatedly
- Water appears from the   external relief/discharge pipe
- You see ceiling/wall damp patches
- You smell gas or suspect combustion issues
